content: Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were conducted in Cameroon, India, Kenya, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe. Among these, one was a randomized controlled trial, seven were cohort studies, four were cross-sectional studies, and one was a pre–post study. Five studies reported exclusive breastfeeding rates at six months, nine studies reported exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months, four studies examined early breastfeeding initiation within one hour of birth, and six studies reported general breastfeeding initiation rates. The randomized controlled trial conducted in South Africa demonstrated improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months but did not show an increase in early breastfeeding initiation rates. Four cohort studies (three of fair quality and one of poor quality) reported improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months following breastfeeding promotion interventions, with two of these improvements being statistically significant. Two low-quality observational studies reported higher exclusive breastfeeding rates at six months among women who received interventions, with a positive dose-response relationship between the number of intervention visits and exclusive breastfeeding rates. Evidence for breastfeeding initiation rates and early initiation was primarily derived from lowto very-low-quality studies. Six observational studies showed increased initiation rates post-intervention, but none included comparison or control groups. The systematic review concluded that breastfeeding promotion and support positively influenced exclusive breastfeeding and initiation rates. Increased frequency of contact was associated with better exclusive breastfeeding practices, with more contacts leading to higher rates. Interventions combining group education and individual counseling, involving fathers and family members, engaging community health workers and trained healthcare workers, and integrating programs for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission with access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) were particularly effective in improving exclusive breastfeeding. No studies were identified that evaluated the impact of interventions on concurrent improvements in ART adherence, although such interventions may have been similar in nature. Additionally, no published studies provided evidence on promoting and supporting safe and adequate replacement feeding practices among mothers living with HIV. In the general population, interventions delivered across multiple settings (health systems, home and family environments, community environments, workplaces, and policy environments) were found to be most effective in improving breastfeeding rates. The greatest improvements in early initiation, exclusive breastfeeding, and continued breastfeeding were observed when counseling or education was provided simultaneously in home and community settings, health systems and community settings, or health systems and home settings. Baby-friendly hospital interventions at the health system level were the most effective in increasing any breastfeeding rates. The authors concluded that improving breastfeeding rates requires delivering interventions across multiple settings, involving health systems, homes, families, and communities concurrently. Indirect evidence from non-HIV-affected populations demonstrated that exclusive and continued breastfeeding rates could be improved through policy-level or health facility and community interventions. Cost-benefit studies were not identified, but the long-term health benefits of such interventions were considered cost-effective. The systematic review also highlighted the importance of clear and consistent messaging to support breastfeeding in the general population, including mothers living with HIV. Training healthcare providers to implement national recommendations on infant feeding and identify women unable to breastfeed for medical reasons was emphasized. National authorities were encouraged to create enabling environments to promote appropriate feeding practices for all infants and young children while scaling up interventions to reduce HIV transmission. In settings where maternal, newborn, and child health services promote breastfeeding and ART to increase HIV-free survival among infants born to mothers living with HIV, mixed feeding with ART was considered better than no breastfeeding at all. However, exclusive breastfeeding remains the recommended practice due to its protective effects against serious childhood illnesses like diarrhea and pneumonia. Antiretroviral drugs significantly reduce the risk of postnatal HIV transmission and appear effective regardless of whether mothers exclusively or partially breastfeed. The Guideline Development Group emphasized that interventions to support safer infant feeding practices are likely to be highly acceptable to mothers living with HIV and health workers. Investments in training and capacity development for health workers to provide counseling and support for early initiation, exclusive breastfeeding, and continued breastfeeding were deemed necessary and cost-effective in the long term. These interventions are also likely to improve health equity, particularly in vulnerable populations, by reducing morbidity and mortality risks associated with suboptimal feeding practices. In summary, the evidence supports the promotion of exclusive breastfeeding and ART among mothers living with HIV to improve infant health outcomes and reduce HIV transmission. Properly designed counseling and support interventions can simultaneously enhance ART adherence and retention in care among mothers living with HIV.
